text.p: The copper price fell through the US$1,900 per tonne support level on Friday night after it failed on the upside earlier in the week as the market moved into contango. Gold and silver prices also weakened, with silver ending at an 18-month low, but oil and wheat prices firmed.
The CRB index ended 0.72 points lower at 244.42.
LME copper prices sagged on Friday to end the week precariously hovering below $1,900 per tonne as a new wave of negative sentiment swept world metals markets.
Speculative sales hit copper again crimping a rally up from $1,850 a week ago -- a level it threatened to revisit after Friday's $36 drop to the LME afternoon close exactly at $1,900.
Copper weakened again by some $20 in late inter-office activity. Dealers cited an emerging contango when forward values are higher than the nearby delivery price.

Copper had been in steep backwardation with spot supply commanding a premium recently when star trader Yasuo Hamanaka, sacked in June by Japan's Sumitomo Corp, was building stocks in an apparent bid to defend a high price.

Traders said the fundamental picture post-Hamanaka is now clearer. Despite falling warehouse stocks and a pick-up in physical interest in Europe, the market now believes that an oversupply in copper will be the feature in 1997.

In a tv interview on Sunday BHP chief executive John Prescott said he would not describe himself as bullish on the copper price and said BHP would have to learn to live with the lower prices. BHP is the world's second largest copper producer.
Aluminium clawed up from Friday's new 2-1/4 year low of $1,403 on end-week covering and technical support.

Traders said the market is likely to fall below $1,400 soon, with fundamentals all depressive. LME warehouse stocks are seen continuing to rise, following Friday's 4,825-tonne increase. Also, August IPAI production data showed output is inching up.

Nickel gradually lost ground during a sluggish session, although price movements were largely low-key and late covering kept losses to a minimum. The 594-tonne stock increase, although expected, also put some pressure on the market.

In the short-term the market will continue to adopt a cautious policy over the ongoing Inco dispute in Canada, although there has been no impcat on supplies so far. Last trade was at $7,380 a tonne, a $10 loss from Thursday's kerb close.
Zinc prices crumbled during the late afternoon, although declines were cushioned just under $1,030, and the market is likely to remain comfortable between $1,030/40.

The 850-tonne stock drawdown was not particularly large, but maintained the recent trend. Zinc ended the kerb at $1,030, down $5.50. Lead also fell away during the afternoon session, reflecting another stock increase, the overall LME trend, and lacklustre conditions. Last business was at $782, down $5.

In the New York bullion market, spot gold saw a two month low at $380.30, before ending quoted around $380.85/381.35, compared to the London afternoon fix Friday of $381.75 and the New York close Thursday at $382.50/383.00. Spot silver slipped to an 18-month low while spot platinum posted a fresh two-month low and palladium set a three-year low.

Both gold and silver are now near the bottom of ranges that have provided value in the past two or three years, analysts noted, and standard nine-day relative strength indicators (RSI) for December gold and December silver closed in oversold zones at 18.43 percent and 18.59 percent respectively.
"There is some concern Russia is having difficulty meeting its budget and may need to sell more commodities to raise revenue," Everen Securities analyst Todd Henrichs said.

"And there's been uncertainty recently about the IMF's plan to sell gold, even though that's been known for some time, but the impetus today came from fund selling after silver fell through the key $5.00 level yesterday," he said.

CBOT wheat futures closed higher on talk of frost in Canadian wheat growing regions which may damage some of the crop, traders said. A late soybean harvest in the U.S. Midwest which could slow seedings of the U.S. soft red winter wheat crop also boosted the market as did concern about wet weather in the U.S. Plains hard red winter region, they said. Short covering also contributed to the advances.

NYMEX oil futures erased most of their early losses, with crude and heating oil settling higher but gasoline again lagged the rest of the oil complex and settled lower, traders said. October crude expired nine cents higher at $23.63 a barrel after slipping to a low $23.26 in afternoon trade, but well above last Friday's settlement of $24.51 a barrel.

CSCE world sugar prices ended a volatile session near the day's lows on continued, technically-driven speculative liquidation, dealers said. The action pushed most-active March contract to a low of 11.19, where a double-bottom has formed on the charts, but the trade proved to be a steady buyer at the lows. The most-active March contract ended off 0.16 at 11.21, having ranged from 11.37 to 11.19. Spot-October slid 0.23 on the day to 11.19. Deferred contracts finished 0.10 to 0.06 weaker.
